expected.question_text: A 35-year-old male presents to the office with the complaints of progressively worsening fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and easy bruising for several weeks. He has no significant past medical history and does not take any medications. expected.explanation_footer:
The laboratory findings and bone marrow biopsy results for this patient are consistent with aplastic anemia . As such, further evaluation would be expected to show an increased erythropoietin (EPO) concentration . Aplastic anemia is a form of bone marrow failure that occurs when hematopoietic stem cells are destroyed by either direct cytotoxic injury or cytotoxic T cells. Loss of these multipotent stem cells results in pancytopenia and clinical manifestations related to anemia (eg, fatigue, pallor), leukopenia (eg, infections), and/or thrombocytopenia (eg, bruising, epistaxis). As a result of stem cell destruction, bone marrow biopsy will show hypocellular marrow with an abundance of lipids. As seen with other forms of anemia, decreased oxygen delivery to tissues results in tissue hypoxia, which will in turn stimulate the production of EPO in the kidney. Therefore, as long as renal function is appropriate (as is the case in this patient with a normal serum creatinine), EPO concentrations will be increased. However, because of the reduced amount of functioning hematologic stem cells, EPO cannot stimulate erythrocytosis, and reticulocytes are inappropriately low. Note that because the erythrocytes produced are normal in size and appearance, evaluation will show a normocytic anemia (normal mean corpuscular volume). The laboratory profile of aplastic anemia is: Pancytopenia with normocytic anemia Increased EPO Decreased reticulocytes No signs of hemolysis (eg, haptoglobin and lactate dehydrogenase concentrations are normal) Aplastic Anemia | Pathophysiology | - Bone marrow failure caused by damage to hematopoietic stem cells | |---|---| | Common causes * | - Autoimmune disease (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus) - Exposure (eg, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, radiation, toxins) - Viral infection (eg, HIV, viral hepatitis) | | Clinical presentation | Patients have complications of pancytopenia, including: - Anemia: dyspnea, fatigue, pallor - Leukopenia: infections - Thrombocytopenia: bleeding and bruising | | Diagnosis | - Normocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count - Peripheral smear: ↓ quantity of morphologically normal cells - Bone marrow biopsy: hypocellular marrow with ↑ stroma and adipocytes | | * Most cases are idiopathic. | |

Aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia with normocytic anemia, decreased reticulocytes, and no signs of hemolysis. Assuming that renal function is normal, erythropoietin concentrations will be increased as a compensatory response to tissue hypoxia.
